elements: 5 wireframe camera frustums uniformly spaced in a horizontal row, all facing right (+X direction)
Black dot (pinhole) at the left vertex (apex) of each frustum
Tall rectangular image plane bounding each frustum on its right side
Faint vertical midline drawn inside each rectangular image plane
Thick red arrows lying on the central axis, placed before the first camera, exactly spanning the gaps between cameras, and continuing after the last camera

interactions.teaches: Rotating the scene reveals that all frusta and arrows are perfectly collinear, demonstrating forward translation strictly along the optical axis with zero sideways velocity.

plan.geometry_notes: Use a global coordinate system where +X is right, +Y is up, and +Z is towards the viewer. Place 5 camera pinholes at X = -8, -4, 0, 4, 8 (spacing of 4 units). Each frustum extends 2 units to the right, with its rectangular image plane at local X + 2. The rectangle has height 3 (Y from -1.5 to 1.5) and width 2 (Z from -1 to 1). Edges are solid black lines. The pinhole is a black sphere of radius 0.15. The midline is a faint grey line (#999999) from Y=1.5 to Y=-1.5 on the image plane at Z=0. The gap between one camera's image plane (e.g., X = -6) and the next pinhole (X = -4) is exactly 2 units. Place thick red arrows (#cc0000) of length exactly 2 units in these gaps so the tail touches the image plane and the tip touches the next pinhole. Add identical arrows from X=-10 to -8, and from X=10 to 12.
plan.notes: Ensure an orthographic/axonometric camera setup so the repeated shapes do not artificially shrink due to perspective depth. Do not add any text labels or interactive highlighting.

authoredPrompt: This figure is a single horizontal strip in which one camera is repeated five times in a row on a white ground, with thick red arrows between and around the copies. Each camera is a black wireframe viewing frustum in three-quarter view: a solid black dot marks the projection center at the left, four straight edges spread rightward from it to the corners of a tall rectangle standing for the image plane, and a faint vertical line inside that rectangle marks its midline. All five frusta match in size and orientation, and every one opens toward the right. A red arrow lies on the axis left of the first camera, another sits in each gap between consecutive cameras, and a final one continues past the last camera to the right edge; all arrowheads point right. Because the arrows run in the same direction the frusta face, the strip shows a camera moving straight ahead down its own optical axis, the case in which the sideways velocity components vanish and only the component along the Z-axis is nonzero.
authoredInteractions:
- Animation for advancing the camera copies along their optical axis; the frustum moves straight through the scene while projected points expand from the image center, linking forward Z translation to radial optical flow.
- Slider for time along the forward path; the active camera position and red direction arrows update together, showing that orientation stays fixed while depth to the scene changes.
- Toggle between the 3-D camera strip and the corresponding image-plane flow field; the visible update switches from rightward frustum motion to outward vectors, clarifying how forward translation becomes expansion in the image.
authoredContext:
For a camera moving forward, as illustrated in

Frustum extends to X+1 with a rectangle of height 1.2 and width 0.8 in the YZ plane. Edges are black lines, pinhole a black sphere radius 0.15, midline grey #999999. Red arrows (length 1.0) placed centered at X = -1.25, 1.25, 3.75, 6.25, 8.75, 11.25. Active camera is rendered in a distinct blue (#1a66cc) and its X position is driven by the 'time' slider (mapped from 0-4 to X=0-10). Reference 3D points are ~20 small spheres at X=15 to 25, randomly scattered in Y, Z within ±4.

Dynamically update the length of the flow vectors based on the distance to the 3D points to accurately reflect standard optical flow equations during translation.
